# How a Shooting Ride Became a Video-Based AI Olympiad Problem
## 1. The Inspiration

On a cloudy day in July 2026, I went to an amusement park with my friends as part of a school trip. We followed a guided tour in the morning that ended inside the park area, and experienced different attractions in the park on our own in the afternoon. One of the attractions that I experienced with my friends was a shooting ride – you sit on a cart and you shoot targets that appear in the scene as it moves through the track. As I struggled to keep my beam steady enough to shoot the targets, I looked down at the display panel, and there was the word “Accuracy” on it. As an AI Olympiad practitioner, I knew something was brewing up.

(sample image of a shooting ride setup)

This shooting-ride set-up looked eerily like one of the IOAI at-home tasks, the Robot Delivery Academy, which asked for a robot to reach a target (the delivery package) and then put it in a designated location on a grid. Both involved an agent trying to reach a target under a success-rate Since video-based tasks had never been assessed in the IOAI before, this was in fact one of my main predictions for the corresponding on-site task for the IOAI (rest assured I didn’t share the full setup to my teammates or my team leaders, since I was already considering submitting such a task to AICC or other public calls for tasks).

Then I started to recall the moments from when we stood in line to when we started the shooting ride. As we waited for the carts to arrive, there was a screen playing an introductory video of the ride, telling us which targets to look for. They only appeared a handful of times in well-cropped form before we had to recognize the targets in the terrain inside the ride. 

The data setup, which contained no labeled training data, only 3 well-cropped images of the targets (one each) and then the videos themselves, was taken almost straight out from there. The temporal modeling component, where I intentionally put a 3-frame delay between “pressing the shoot button” and “the beam actually reaching the target”, came from my experience getting accustomed to the movements of the cart during my reaction time when firing the beams. The task ended up being,

> "Given the first 25 frames (indices 0–24) of a video, where one of the three targets moves together with the background, predict a coordinate in pixel space such that it lies on that target in frame 27 (0-indexed)."

Later on when I was scrolling through my social media feed (which contains quite a large proportion of AI/ML-related reels), I watched a video of how drones use their visual systems to avoid the obstacles ahead, then I realized that my problem setup was quite related to the predictive modeling in real-time systems. You need to forecast where the obstacle will be after some time delay, not simply point out where the obstacle is now, in order to avoid it by adjusting the trajectory of an already moving frame.

This comes to the first takeaway in this blog post: Next time you go on trips, or when you hang out and play games with friends, immerse yourself in the experience and pay some attention to what you’re executing, as they are very good inspirations for tasks. They are very good food for thought for AI-related ideas, especially with embodied AI as you literally engage in tasks which require coordinating a good amount of complexity of movements, the same coordination that researchers have been trying to write down in mathematical optimizations and algorithms so that they can also be done in autonomous systems.

P.S.: The “Who Are the Impostors” problem from AICC Beginner Round 0, which I authored, was inspired by experience playing Among Us with my friends and exploring the features in the game.
## 2. Task Development

After the amusement park visit, I began developing this task during the final phases of my IOAI preparation, and continued after the competition as I saw a public call for tasks coming from FAIO (Fizmat AI Olympiad), an international AI Olympiad competition featuring a unique team-based format (the IOAI also features a team challenge, but in the FAIO all contests are conducted directly between teams of 1 to 3, not individuals). 

A few weeks after I submitted the problem, titled The Mysterious Shooting Ride, to the call-for-tasks Google form, the organizers and the jury members of the contest arranged a meeting with me to discuss my problem. 

Initially, the metric came from the ride itself too. There was literally the word “accuracy” on the display panel on the cart. So in the initial version, I simply used hit-or-miss accuracy, and had all videos contain a target so that false positives or false negatives in terms of whether to shoot are not possible. But then the jury asked a question that went like, “would it be a good idea if you reward contestants who get it dead center with a higher score than those who skimmed every target on the edges?” They suggested using a scoring system like a game of darts – you score full points if you predict the exact center of the object, and the partial credits linearly decay as your distance from the object center increases. Of course, there’s no credit when your prediction misses the target altogether.

My initial set-up also came with a simple movement pattern of the entire frame – a figure eight. If somebody noticed that the motion is sinusoidal on both axes, that’s (at least conceptually) it – the score would only depend on the accuracy of the detection, not the temporal modeling. So the jury suggested using different classes of movements, and I ended up blending some of them together in my final dataset – incorporating polynomial splines, figure-eight, and ellipsoidal movements while simultaneously zooming in and out in each video.

As the official [IOAI 2027 task development guidelines](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1smxkjkzOypsaQ9IKCBNa6sfa17PGS84lCUqIFGBkV_8/edit?tab=t.vdf5trcvci47) say, “Stay ready to change everything but the core” – there were quite some aspects, including the scoring and the dataset, that had to be amended (as mentioned above). But I managed to keep the core of the task, the three-phase modeling*, intact – until the testing phase.
## 3. How It Managed to Stay Mysterious
### 3.1 The Solutions

This problem wasn’t developed in a top-down approach where I get inspired by a particular elegant methodology, then I scaffold a problem around that idea. It was a bottom-up approach in which I observe an interesting problem and try to solve it like how a contestant would and refine and debug the problem on the way. So it took me quite a lot of time (at least 8 hours, and more if you count the initial versions of the problem that got iterated away) to develop my intended solution, and when I got approximately 39 points (since further improved) and presented it to a follow-up meeting, I thought I could finally breathe easy.

For my intended solution, I started from constructing a synthetic dataset to fine-tune a pretrained YOLO checkpoint. But then there are a lot of details to be careful about. For instance, if the supplied target images are pasted directly to the video frames, there would be very easy-to-identify black edges around the targets. This would provide a shortcut for the model to recognize an obvious cue that would fail on the actual videos without the black borders in the middle of frames. It is also a good idea to freeze the early layers of the YOLO model in the initial training phase to prevent it from overfitting to the synthetic dataset, which no matter how realistically constructed would still differ from the actual distribution of targets in real videos. Then for the temporal modeling part, I constructed a pipeline involving training a PyTorch LSTM after some very careful data normalization work.

I wanted this task to assess not just the general knowledge about what methods to apply for which data scenarios, but also the detail-mindedness of the contestants when working with data – something that I lacked and cost me at least 55 points in the very first task of IOAI 2026.

I got even more excited when Agzam, the tester of my task,
got a higher score (at least 65 points, and up to 85 points in a model ensemble) after about 4-5 hours testing it, using a different approach. To quote what he said, 

> "UNet looks at each frame and marks spots that look like the target. The whole video slowly zooms and pans in a smooth sinusoidal pattern, and the target moves with it. We undo that motion for all 25 frames the real target lands on the same spot each time, while false detections scatter. Then we continue the sinusoidal pattern 3 frames ahead to predict where the target will be at frame 27.”
> 

The synthetic data construction step stayed, but instead of fine-tuning an object detection model, a semantic segmentation model is trained from scratch on pixel-level maps of the target.
### 3.2 What Went Wrong

But then I found myself asking a question a few days after that: would the pretrained YOLO model in my intended solution be provided to contestants? I thought, if the amazing tester for my task trained a UNet architecture from scratch and got a higher score than I did, why should I ask more? If the pretrained models were to be incorporated into the task environment, would that create a hassle for the testers to have to re-test my task from scratch?

I briefly brought up the topic of pretrained models (albeit somewhat indirectly I suspect, since I also mentioned which documentation to give out to contestants) to the organizers a few days before the contest, but the contest environment that the testers tested was already getting shipped into the actual contest. Guess what was the highest score (out of 100) in The Mysterious Shooting Ride in FAIO 2026?

Well, that was still a nontrivial effort as it turned out the pretrained models were not available in the task environment. I struggled to score above 3 points for hours as I debugged my pretrained YOLO model setup in the initial stages of the task development. It was just too hard, even for teams of up to 3, to score double digits in this problem while juggling 3 other problems in a 5-hour contest day.
### 3.3 Takeaways

Perhaps some of the most valuable lessons from the process developing this task, which ended up much more challenging than I intended, are less about AI Olympiad preparation and more about general work ethic. 

1. If anything seems off, just ask the organizers or higher-ups instead of assuming anything, even if that seems annoying to them. This is especially important in safety-critical situations, and reminds me of the videos about aviation disasters I watched when I was younger, ‘where one question that didn’t get asked, one assumption that didn’t actually hold true, allowed holes in a Swiss cheese to line up and caused real incidents.

2. If you can think of which steps to take in order to make the situation clearer to your colleagues, go the extra mile and do it. For instance, task authors, put your author solution notebooks and materials together and hand them in, even if the organizers don’t require you to.
